title: Advanced Filtering Patterns
learning_outcomes: Explain how advanced filtering patterns affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from date and timestamp ranges to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on advanced filtering patterns in filtering, sorting, searching, and pagination. You will connect date and timestamp ranges to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Advanced Filtering Patterns matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying date and timestamp ranges deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Collection endpoints need explicit parameter validation, stable ordering, bounded result sizes, and predictable pagination metadata. In this lesson, treat “Advanced Filtering Patterns” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Concepts to connect
items: Whitelist supported filters and sort fields

Accept: application/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"items": [], "next_cursor": null}

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Date and timestamp ranges”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Nested properties” and “Validation of complex query syntax”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Bound query cost and make ordering stable before adding more expressive query options. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating advanced filtering patterns as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
